title: Water a house plant at its roots without wetting its leaves
instruction: Water the plant at its roots, onto the soil, without wetting its leaves. Then put the jug back on its stool, leave the plant's leaves as they were and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Many house plants (and seedlings, and vegetables in a bed) must be watered at the soil, not over the leaves, which rot or scorch when wet; with leaves spread over the pot, one hand holds the foliage aside while the other pours, as in caring for plants at home, in a nursery or in a care home.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A terracotta pot 17 cm across and 7.5 cm tall on a saucer, its middle 30 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, filled with dark soil 1.3 cm below its rim; fixed. In it a house plant with a green stem and broad leaves (15 cm long, up to 13 cm wide) spread low over the soil: three fixed in the crown, over the back and both sides of the pot, and one big leaf in front on a springy stalk, joined to the stem 10 cm above the table, lying over the front of the soil and reaching out 6 cm past the rim toward the arms. Pushed round on its stalk, the big leaf springs back over the soil when let go. (2) A blue plastic watering jug (5.4 cm across, 8.5 cm tall, with a pouring lip and a handle) holding 120 ml of water, simulated as 12 drops (7 mm beads, 10 ml each), standing on a beech stool 6 cm tall, 26 cm forward and 13 cm left of the centre line. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: an artificial house plant built to the sizes above, so every trial has the same leaves in the same places. Its four leaves are white cellulose sponge cloth (the Swedish-dishcloth type, 70% cellulose and 30% cotton, which its makers rate to absorb up to 15 times its own weight; a 17.5 x 20 cm cloth weighs about 9 g): each is four layers cut to the 141 cm² blade outline and stitched round the edge, about 14.5 g dry, so it holds up to about 217 ml, more than the whole 120 ml. Each leaf is clipped to a wire stalk: the three crown leaves over the back and sides, and the big lower leaf on a sprung wire stalk lying over the front of the soil, which springs back when let go. It stands in real potting soil, just moist, in the same 17 cm glazed terracotta pot on its saucer, with the drainage hole plugged by a rubber bung for the trial. The jug (about 150 ml) holds 120 ml of room-temperature water tinted dark blue with food colouring (about 1 ml per litre), so a drop that touches a leaf leaves a blue stain on the white cloth. (The simulation draws the leaves green.)
scoring: Judged at the end. Real trial (1 g of water = 1 ml), two separate measurements: (a) water delivered to the soil: the pot is weighed in the same state before and after, with all four cloth leaves unclipped (it keeps its soil, stem, wire stalks, clips and bung). Before the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out of its saucer and weigh it, and the dry saucer, on a kitchen scale (1 g steps), then clip the leaves back on; after the trial, unclip the leaves again (into their bags, below), lift the pot out, let it drip into the saucer, and weigh the pot and the saucer. The pot's gain is the water delivered to the soil (its drainage hole is plugged, and the 1.3 cm of headroom above the soil holds about 235 ml, so none leaves the pot); the saucer's gain is spilled water and never counts as delivered. (b) water that touched the leaves, recorded two ways: by weight, each leaf weighed dry before the trial and, after it, unclipped into its own pre-weighed clear sealed bag and weighed on a 0.01 g scale, their total gain being the leaf water (each leaf holds more than the whole 120 ml, so none can be overfilled); and by stain, every leaf photographed on both faces through its bag, since the dyed water stains the white cloth wherever it touches, however fast it comes and whether or not the cloth keeps it. Any stain counts as leaf contact and is scored with the weights: a stain that runs over a leaf's edge (water left the leaf unweighed) counts as more than 10 ml, whatever the leaves gained. Before trials the operator validates the leaves (a procedure to run, not a result we have measured): with a dry, weighed leaf clipped on its stalk at its trial angle over a pre-weighed tray, pour 10 ml onto its middle from the trial jug held 5 cm above it and tipped over as fast as it goes, and 120 ml the same way onto a second dry leaf; each leaf must keep at least 98% of what was poured (a gain of at least 9.8 g and 117.6 g; the tray catches the rest) and show a stain, and the 10 ml stain must not reach the edge. If a leaf fails, every leaf gets another layer of cloth and the check is repeated. Simulation: each of the 12 beads stands for 10 ml. A bead counts as leaf water if it ever comes within 4 mm of any leaf, checked after every physics step (240 times a second); it counts as delivered only if it ends lying on the soil inside the pot's wall (its centre within 7.25 cm of the pot's axis and between 3 mm below and 15 mm above the soil's surface) without ever having touched a leaf. Beads that miss the pot, bounce out of it or land in the saucer never count. 1.0: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads) and at most 10 ml on the leaves (cloth leaves gain at most 10 g, with no stain running over an edge; 1 bead), the jug back on its stool (within 3 cm, upright within 15 degrees), the big leaf back over the soil (within 12 degrees of where it lay), both hands let go (each TCP at least 4 cm from the jug and the leaf) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm); in a real trial the end state is checked against marks on the stool and the pot's rim (ruler and protractor) and the robot's joint log. 0.5: the same amounts of water, without the end state. 0.25: at least 40 ml delivered (pot gain at least 40 g; 4 beads). Else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the jug, the big leaf and every bead still.
reset_notes: Pull the bung and let the pot drain, then plug it again (it is weighed afresh, leaves unclipped, before each trial); empty and dry the saucer; clip on fresh, dry, unstained, pre-weighed cloth leaves; lay the big leaf back over the soil; refill the jug with 120 ml of the dyed water and stand it on its stool.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the 120 ml of water is 12 rigid 7 mm beads (10 ml each, 0.8 g) that do not soak in or cling; a real trial weighs the leafless pot, the saucer and the cloth leaves, and dyed water stains any leaf it touches. The saucer is drawn only. Leaves are rigid green plates (white cloth in a real trial); the crown's leaves and the pot are fixed, and the big leaf turns on its stalk against a spring (0.0016 N m per degree).
